summary: The breakwater light at Indiana Harbor: a 1924 crib-and-concrete light was replaced by a 1935 art deco tower on the extended breakwater; the old one was demolished.

lens.where: replaced by a modern green beacon (LighthouseFriends)

structures.type: square light tower with lantern and gallery on a two-story keeper dwelling, on a concrete pier
structures.note: Reinforced-concrete frame with brick curtain walls (Bureau description, via LighthouseFriends); demolished by the Coast Guard, 1980s.

structures.type: art deco tower on arched concrete base
structures.note: LighthouseFriends and Wikipedia describe steel; the Archive records concrete (see notes).

structures.type: cylindrical D9 tower on the original pier

access.note: Coast Guard property at the end of an industrial breakwater in a private industrial area; best seen from the water. Not open to the public (Archive).

events.note: First lights at Indiana Harbor: two skeletal metal towers on enclosed bases, one at the outer end of a breakwater, the other shoreward to form range lights
Stone-filled crib for the main light completed August 1920 by Army engineers; steel-tower east pierhead light exhibited 5 June 1920
West breakwater light, a 31-ft steel tower with automatic acetylene light, commenced operation 14 July 1923 (not the main light)
Main light at the end of the east breakwater activated 2 May 1924: fourth-order lens, two white flashes every 20 seconds
Illuminant changed from oil vapor to electricity
Art deco tower on arched concrete base at the outermost point of the breakwater extended 1934-1935
New tower took the breakwater light name; the 1924 light became the inner light
Radiobeacon installed as an additional aid for mariners
Original 1924 light demolished by the Coast Guard, in the 1980s (no exact year in either source)
Cylindrical D9 tower on the original pier, marked Indiana Harbor Light 5 (Rowlett)

corrections.proposed: Iso G 6s (three seconds on, three seconds off)
corrections.why: LighthouseFriends describes the modern green beacon on the 1935 tower as three seconds on and three seconds off. Not verified against the current Light List.

14.6 m (48 ft) is Rowlett directory figure for the cylindrical D9 Light 5 on the original pier. LighthouseFriends gives the original 1935 lens a focal plane of 78 feet (23.8 m). The current focal height is not verified.
LighthouseFriends dates the main light at the end of the east breakwater to 2 May 1924. The 1923 date belongs to the west breakwater light (14 July 1923) or to the Rowlett directory station date.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1923 date in the record and in Rowlett corresponds to the west breakwater light (commenced 14 July 1923, LighthouseFriends); the main light at the end of the east breakwater was activated 2 May 1924. The Archive gives 1924 for the first light of the old place record.

The Archive lists the 1924 light as not existing ("Existing: No"). LighthouseFriends describes a modern green beacon lit on the 1935 art deco tower today. The inactive status belongs to the demolished 1924 light, while the 1935 tower is active.

notes_for_editor: (1) Two Archive place records. The current light's record (place 'Indiana Harbor East Breakwater', est. 1935) holds one roster line, Edward C. Peterson (-1925), second assistant, which predates its establishment; the 40-line roster sits on the 'Old' record (est. 1924). The keepers table treats all 41 lines as this station's keepers, since LighthouseFriends says the old station's keepers ran the new light by cable. (2) Tower material: the Archive says concrete on a stone-filled crib; LighthouseFriends says steel on an arched concrete base. Unresolved; the story states both. Wikipedia (lead only) says Art Deco steel, 23 m (75 ft), isophase green 6s, focal height 78 ft, not cited. (3) The record's 'Fl G 2.5s', focal height 14.6 m, range 5.2 nm and 'fog signal: horn' match Rowlett's cylindrical D9 'Light 5' on the original pier (1985), not the 1935 tower. The record's fog-signal entry is not sourced here. Corrections are proposed, not applied. (4) First lit: Rowlett gives station established 1923; LighthouseFriends gives the west breakwater light 14 July 1923 and the main light 2 May 1924. The story and facts use 1924 for the main light. (5) The 1920 East Pierhead light (steel tower, lit 5 June 1920) is a separate aid per LighthouseFriends and the Commissioner's 1920 report; it is mentioned in the story only as LighthouseFriends gives it. (6) Name variants: 'James C. Peitersen' (Archive) and 'James C. Peiterson' (LighthouseFriends); 'Stanley William Clarke' (Archive) and 'Stanley W. Clark' (LighthouseFriends). The story uses the Archive spelling. (7) Coast Guard personnel on the 'USCG' heading (1950s to 1968) appear in the keepers table as the Archive prints them. The story names none of them. (8) The 1921 Commissioner report (scan page 657) gives 'completed in August, 1920'; the printed page was not confirmed. The 1917, 1919 and 1920 passages were read from scan pages with printed pages marked as read. (9) Storms, wrecks and rescues: none found in the sources read, so the chapter is omitted. Two newspaper searches (1923-1925) found nothing about the light. (10) Not verified beyond LighthouseFriends: the 1934-1935 extension, the 1952 radiobeacon, the 1929 electrification, the 1980s demolition and the 1985 D9 date (Rowlett). The 1907 Board reply is taken from LighthouseFriends' summary; the Board's report is not in the corpus. (11) The record says 'boat only'; that is not sourced here. LighthouseFriends says the light is best seen from the water, and the story uses its words. (12) No photos added. Verification pass 2026-10-27: south-arm tower placement corrected to the 1917 report (north end of the south arm); Rowlett's 1923 station date added as a disagreement with LighthouseFriends' 1924; LighthouseFriends quotes shortened or paraphrased, and units added for the breakwater extension and focal plane.
